name: Deep Vein Thrombosis
cards: Define deep vein thrombosis.
Clot formation in the deep veins, usually in the legs.
What share of all deep vein thromboses occur in the upper extremity?
Lower extremity deep vein thrombosis is how many times more common than upper extremity?
About ten times.
Most common causes of upper extremity deep vein thrombosis?
Pacemakers, implantable defibrillators and indwelling central venous catheters.
Pulmonary embolism rate: upper versus lower extremity thrombosis?
Up to 6% versus 15% to 30%.
Where does lower extremity deep vein thrombosis usually begin?
In the calf, then it moves proximally.
Most common proximal veins affected in the leg?
Femoral and popliteal veins in the thigh.
Most common distal veins affected in the leg?
Peroneal veins in the calf.
Which veins are affected during pregnancy?
Pelvic veins.
Age threshold listed as a risk factor for deep vein thrombosis?
Older than 60 years.
Which bowel diseases raise deep vein thrombosis risk?
Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
How much does a prior deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism raise recurrence risk?
Several-fold higher, roughly 3 to 10 times.
Postpartum window of raised deep vein thrombosis risk?
The first 6 to 12 weeks.
Which leg symptom is most sensitive for deep vein thrombosis?
Swelling, at 97% sensitivity.
Sensitivity of leg pain and of leg warmth?
86% and 72%, respectively.
Classic calf complaint that persists and worsens over days?
A cramp or charley horse in the lower calf.
Define the Homan sign.
Calf pain on dorsiflexion of the foot.
How reliable is the Homan sign?
Neither sensitive nor specific.
Symptom pattern of an isolated distal deep vein thrombosis?
Symptoms confined to the calf.
Which mimic causes severe sudden calf discomfort?
Ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst.
Which mimic causes leg pain with redness, fever and chills?
Cellulitis.
Post-thrombotic syndrome appears how long after a deep vein thrombosis?
6 to 24 months.
Which mimic follows pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation?
Lymphedema.
Historic gold standard, replaced by duplex ultrasound?
Contrast ascending venography.
Fatal pulmonary embolism rate, untreated deep vein thrombosis without embolism?
Under 1%.
Fatal rate, untreated symptomatic nonmassive pulmonary embolism?
Fatal rate, untreated symptomatic massive pulmonary embolism?
About 9%.
Mainstay of deep vein thrombosis treatment?
Anticoagulation.
Classic anticoagulation strategy for deep vein thrombosis?
Heparin, then bridge to warfarin.
Which drug class is dabigatran?
Direct thrombin inhibitor.
Which drug class are rivaroxaban and apixaban?
Direct factor Xa inhibitors.
Which drugs follow 5 days of parenteral therapy?
Dabigatran or edoxaban.
Contraindications to anticoagulation?
Active bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, major trauma, severe bleeding disorders.
Duration when a major transient risk factor provoked the clot?
3 months.
Duration when a minor transient risk factor provoked the clot?
3 to 6 months.
Duration for an unprovoked first venous thromboembolism?
Indefinite.
Which patients may be treated as outpatients?
Stable, low bleeding risk, normal kidneys, reliable follow-up.
Warfarin overlap with heparin lasts until when?
International normalized ratio above 2 for at least 24 hours.
Reversal agent for heparin?
Protamine sulfate.
Reversal agent for dabigatran?
Idarucizumab.
Reversal agent for apixaban and rivaroxaban?
Andexanet alfa.
Only indication for an inferior vena cava filter?
Acute proximal leg thrombosis with bleeding or anticoagulant contraindication.
Which thrombolytic drug treats large proximal thrombosis?
Tissue plasminogen activator.
Which device prevents thrombosis in immobilized hospital patients?
Intermittent pneumatic compression.
Most feared complication of deep vein thrombosis?
Pulmonary embolism.

name: Virchow Triad & Wells Criteria
cards: Name the three parts of the Virchow triad.
Venous stasis, hypercoagulable state, endothelial trauma.
Which Virchow component means altered blood flow?
Venous stasis.
Which Virchow component means inherited or acquired clotting tendency?
Hypercoagulable state.
Which Virchow component means injury to the vessel wall?
Endothelial trauma.
Prolonged sitting and postoperative inactivity fit which Virchow component?
Venous stasis.
How much does immobilization raise deep vein thrombosis risk?
About 20 times.
Venous insufficiency and heart failure fit which Virchow component?
Venous stasis.
Factor V Leiden fits which Virchow component?
Hypercoagulable state.
Inherited defects listed under the hypercoagulable component?
Factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C or S deficiency, antithrombin deficiency.
Cancer and pregnancy fit which Virchow component?
Hypercoagulable state.
Estrogen exposures listed under the hypercoagulable component?
Oral contraceptives and postmenopausal estrogen replacement.
What makes oral contraceptive risk even higher?
Tobacco smoking or obesity.
Trauma and burns fit which Virchow component?
Endothelial trauma.
Surgeries carrying the greatest deep vein thrombosis risk?
Knee replacement, hip replacement and hip fracture surgery.
Which drug use injures lower extremity veins?
Intravenous drug use.
In what settings is the Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis used?
Outpatient and emergency department.
In which setting is the Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis NOT used?
Inpatient (hospitalized) patients.
What does the Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis estimate?
Pretest probability of deep vein thrombosis.
How many points is each positive Wells item usually worth?
One point.
Which Wells item subtracts points, and how many?
Alternative diagnosis as likely as thrombosis: minus two.
Wells cancer item: treatment or palliation within what time?
Within 6 months.
Wells item: bedridden for longer than what?
More than 3 days.
Wells item: major surgery within what time?
Within 12 weeks.
Wells calf swelling item: larger than the other leg by what?
More than 3 centimeters.
Where is Wells calf circumference measured?
10 centimeters below the tibial tuberosity.
Which superficial veins score in the Wells criteria?
Collateral (nonvaricose) superficial veins.
Wells swelling item covering the whole limb?
Entire leg swollen.
Which tenderness scores in the Wells criteria?
Localized along the deep venous system.
Which edema scores in the Wells criteria?
Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg.
Which limb items score under Wells paralysis or immobilization?
Paralysis, paresis or recent plaster immobilization of the leg.
Does a previously documented deep vein thrombosis score in Wells?
Yes, one point.
Does long travel score as Wells immobilization?
No; only bedridden, surgery or cast counts.
Is a positive Homan sign a Wells item?
No.
Do pregnancy and estrogen therapy score in Wells?
No; they are not Wells items.
Wells category for a score below zero?
Low likelihood.
Wells category for a score of 1 to 2?
Moderate likelihood.
Wells category for a score of 3 or greater?
High likelihood.
Approximate deep vein thrombosis prevalence at a Wells score below zero?
About 5%.
Approximate pretest probability at a Wells score of 1 to 2?
About 17%.
First test for a low Wells score?
D-dimer.
First test for a moderate Wells score?
D-dimer.
Which test follows a high Wells score?
Ultrasound, skipping the D-dimer.
What does an elevated D-dimer imply?
Increased fibrinolysis.
How does the D-dimer perform diagnostically?
Sensitive but not specific.
Best use of the D-dimer for deep vein thrombosis?
Rule-out test.
Low Wells score with a negative D-dimer means what?
Stop; deep vein thrombosis is ruled out.
Low Wells score with a positive D-dimer means what?
Order an ultrasound.
Does a positive D-dimer confirm deep vein thrombosis?
No; it shows fibrinolysis somewhere.
Negative ultrasound with high Wells score: repeat ultrasound when?
In 1 week.
Other options after a negative thigh ultrasound with high risk?
Lower leg ultrasound or phlebography.

name: Chronic Venous Insufficiency & Varicose Veins
cards: Spectrum of chronic venous disease from mild to severe?
Telangiectasias, varicose veins, chronic venous insufficiency.
Another name for chronic venous insufficiency?
Postthrombotic syndrome.
What underlies chronic venous disease?
Venous hypertension.
Causes of venous hypertension?
Poor muscle pump, incompetent valves, thrombosis, nonthrombotic obstruction.
What relieves chronic venous disease symptoms?
Limb elevation and walking.
Cause of brown or blue-gray skin discoloration?
Hemosiderin deposits.
Signs marking advanced chronic venous insufficiency?
Edema, skin changes, venous ulceration.
Define lipodermatosclerosis.
Skin and fat scarring in the lower legs.
Define primary chronic venous insufficiency.
Intrinsic vein wall or valve abnormality causing reflux.
Define secondary chronic venous insufficiency.
Obstruction or valve incompetence after a prior deep vein thrombosis.
Most common cause of chronic venous insufficiency?
Prior deep vein thrombosis.
Share of patients with no known deep vein thrombosis history?
Another common cause besides prior thrombosis?
Progressive superficial venous reflux.
What happens to valve leaflets in postthrombotic syndrome?
They become thickened and scarred.
Primary presenting symptom of chronic venous insufficiency?
Progressive pitting edema of the lower leg.
Describe the stasis dermatitis rash.
Eczematous with erythema, scaling, weeping and crusting.
Usual location of a venous ulcer?
Above the ankle, medial or anterior.
How does chronic venous insufficiency cellulitis appear?
Blanching erythema, with or without pain.
Which diseases cause bilateral leg edema mimicking venous insufficiency?
Heart failure, chronic kidney disease, decompensated liver disease.
Which drug classes cause leg edema?
Calcium channel blockers, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, thiazolidinediones.
Unilateral swelling with absent varicosities suggests which condition?
Lymphedema.
Bilateral symmetric edema just above ankles in women?
Lipedema.
Test assessing venous patency and valve competence?
Venous duplex ultrasound.
Which test precedes compression for a leg wound?
Ankle-brachial index.
Why is the ankle-brachial index checked before compression?
Compression is contraindicated in peripheral artery disease.
Gold standard for chronic venous disease, rarely needed?
Catheter-based venography.
Initial management of chronic venous insufficiency?
Skin care, leg elevation, exercise, compression.
How high should legs be elevated?
Above heart level.
Standard treatment for chronic venous insufficiency?
Compression therapy.
Where is graduated compression pressure greatest?
At the ankle.
Which antibiotics treat cellulitis in chronic venous insufficiency?
Cephalexin or clindamycin.
What must happen before a venous ulcer will heal?
Edema controlled and compression applied.
Which oral drug may speed ulcer healing?
Aspirin.
Which drugs treat inflamed stasis dermatitis?
Mid-potency topical corticosteroids.
Downside of valvuloplasty?
High postoperative rate of deep vein thrombosis.
Which findings prompt vascular specialist referral?
Arterial insufficiency, nonhealing or recurrent ulcers, significant saphenous reflux.
What combination produces varicose veins?
Venous reflux plus venous hypertension.
Most commonly involved varicose vein?
The great saphenous vein.
Most common predisposing factor for varicose veins?
Family history.
Activities that raise venous pressure and cause varicose veins?
Prolonged standing and heavy lifting.
Most common varicose vein symptom?
Dull, achy heaviness brought on by standing.
Long-standing varicose veins can progress to what?
Chronic venous insufficiency.
Varicose vein diagnosis is mainly what?
Clinical, with the leg dependent.
Conservative therapy for isolated varicose veins?
Elevation, exercise and compression.
Define sclerotherapy.
Injecting an agent to fibrose and obliterate veins.
Surgical options for varicose vein reflux?
Vein stripping, laser or radiofrequency catheter.

name: Thrombophlebitis & Arteriovenous Fistula
cards: Define superficial phlebitis.
Inflammation of the vein wall without thrombus.
Define superficial thrombophlebitis.
Phlebitis with thrombus.
Most common cause of lower extremity thrombophlebitis?
Varicose veins.
Most common cause of upper extremity thrombophlebitis?
Recent intravenous catheter use.
Which catheter is most often responsible?
Peripherally inserted central catheter.
Hormonal risk factors for thrombophlebitis?
Pregnancy or estrogen therapy.
Which lower extremity history also raises thrombophlebitis risk?
Superficial vein thrombosis without varicose veins.
Findings along a phlebitic vein?
Tenderness, pain, induration and erythema.
Classic palpable finding in thrombophlebitis?
An indurated cord along a superficial vein.
Findings suggesting septic thrombophlebitis?
High fever, fluctuance or purulent drainage.
Which erythema pattern suggests septic thrombophlebitis?
Erythema extending well beyond the vein margin.
Septic thrombophlebitis is uncommon without what history?
Venous cannulation.
Confirmatory test for thrombophlebitis?
Venous duplex ultrasound.
Duplex finding in thrombophlebitis?
Noncompressible vein with clot and thick wall.
Ultrasound wall thickening alone means what?
Phlebitis.
Ultrasound wall thickening with clot means what?
Thrombophlebitis.
How often does thrombophlebitis cause serious complications?
Rarely.
How often does superficial thrombophlebitis embolize?
Rarely.
Typical thrombophlebitis treatment?
Warm compresses, compression, elevation and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Which nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are examples for thrombophlebitis?
Ibuprofen and diclofenac.
When may anticoagulation be started?
Extensive clot burden or intermediate or higher thrombosis risk.
Anticoagulants named for thrombophlebitis?
Unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin, fondaparinux.
When should thrombophlebitis be re-examined?
Within 7 to 10 days.
What follows persistent or worsening signs?
Repeat duplex ultrasound.
Define an arteriovenous fistula.
Abnormal connection between an artery and a vein.
What does an arteriovenous fistula bypass?
The capillary bed.
Where are upper extremity fistulas most often created?
For hemodialysis vascular access.
Most common cause of lower extremity fistulas?
Iatrogenic, from groin vascular access.
Preferred sites for a created hemodialysis fistula?
Upper arm or forearm.
What does a healthy fistula do with arm elevation?
Collapses completely.
Findings in a healthy dialysis fistula?
Diffuse thrill and soft bruit.
Timing of the bruit in a healthy fistula?
Both systolic and diastolic.
Which vessels does an iatrogenic fistula usually affect?
Femoral vessels.
What should follow a groin puncture?
Complete leg vascular exam comparing pulses with baseline.
Test confirming a suspected iatrogenic fistula?
Duplex ultrasound.
How is an arteriovenous fistula usually diagnosed?
Physical examination.
Complications to watch for with a fistula?
Infection, venous insufficiency, heart failure, ischemia.
Define the Nicoladoni-Branham sign.
Reflex slowing of heart rate on compressing a large fistula.
Imaging that confirms a fistula's location and size?
Computed tomography angiography or angiography.
Why is congenital fistula hard to treat?
Communications are numerous.
Conservative treatment of congenital fistula?
Elastic support hose.
Procedure that can remove a congenital fistula?
Embolization.
Treatment of an acquired fistula?
Surgery to remove it or shrink it.

name: Peripheral Artery Disease & Critical Limb Ischemia
cards: Define peripheral arterial disease.
Lack of blood flow to muscle relative to its metabolism, causing pain in those muscles.
Three segmental sites of lower-extremity arterial disease?
Aortoiliac, femoral-popliteal and tibial segments.
Age threshold for peripheral arterial disease without other risk factors?
Over 60 years old.
Age threshold for peripheral arterial disease with risk factors?
50 years old.
How much does smoking raise peripheral arterial disease risk?
Three times the risk of nonsmokers.
Which amino acid is linked to earlier-onset atherosclerosis?
Homocysteine.
What share of patients with peripheral arterial disease also have coronary artery disease?
Define intermittent claudication.
Muscle pain with activity, relieved by rest, usually within 10 minutes.
Commonest site of claudication?
The calf.
Upper two-thirds calf claudication points to which artery?
Superficial femoral artery.
Lower third calf claudication points to which artery?
Popliteal artery.
Buttock and hip claudication points to which segment?
Aortoiliac disease.
Leriche syndrome triad?
Claudication, absent or diminished femoral pulses, erectile dysfunction.
Skin and appendage findings in chronic limb ischemia?
Dry, thin, shiny skin with hair loss and brittle nails.
Define dependent rubor.
Deep red discoloration of the leg when it hangs down.
Buerger test, first step?
Elevate the leg to 45 degrees for one minute and look for pallor.
In darker skin, what replaces color in the Buerger test?
Temperature, skin texture and capillary refill.
Capillary refill threshold suggesting arterial disease?
Longer than 2 seconds.
Important simple bedside initial test for peripheral arterial disease?
Ankle-brachial index.
Ankle-brachial index band for claudication?
Ankle-brachial index band for rest pain and tissue loss?
What does an ankle-brachial index above 1.3 mean?
Calcified, noncompressible arteries, for example in diabetes.
Mainstay initial imaging when arterial stenosis is suspected?
Duplex ultrasound.
Gold standard test for peripheral arterial disease?
Conventional angiography.
Blood pressure goal in peripheral arterial disease with diabetes?
Below 130/80 mmHg.
Minimum exercise prescription for claudication?
30 to 45 minutes, three times a week, ideally supervised.
Antiplatelet that is also a vasodilator?
Cilostazol.
Treatment for hyperhomocysteinemia?
Folic acid with vitamins B12 and B6; it lowers homocysteine but has not cut heart attacks or strokes.
When is revascularization recommended for claudication?
Severe functional disability despite exercise or drug therapy.
Rest pain: where and when is it worst?
Forefoot and toes, on elevation or reclining, often at night.
What relieves ischemic rest pain?
Hanging the leg over the bed edge or walking around.
Typical arterial ulcer appearance?
Dry, punched out, painful, minimal bleeding at the toe tips.
Wet gangrene is what kind of problem?
A surgical emergency, with infection and risk of sepsis.
Principal use of a bypass graft?
Severe critical leg ischemia.

name: Acute Limb Ischemia, Atheroembolism & Carotid Disease
cards: Define acute limb ischemia.
Sudden occlusion of a previously patent artery; a vascular emergency.
Most common embolic source in acute limb ischemia?
The heart, in 80% to 90% of cases.
Two cardiac sources of limb emboli?
Atrial fibrillation and left ventricular thrombus after myocardial infarction.
The six P's of arterial assessment?
Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia.
Define poikilothermia.
Difficulty regulating body temperature.
Often the earliest neurologic sign of acute limb ischemia?
Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.
Rutherford category I?
Viable: no sensory loss or weakness, Doppler signals audible.
Rutherford category IIB prognosis?
Salvageable only with immediate revascularization.
Where is a category IIB limb evaluated and treated?
In a surgical suite.
Rutherford category III outcome?
Major amputation regardless of therapy.
First two actions in acute limb ischemia?
Immediate vascular surgery consult and intravenous heparin.
Time limit for catheter-directed thrombolysis?
Acute limb ischemia under 14 days' duration.
Thrombolytic drug named for acute limb ischemia?
Alteplase.
What embolizes in atheroembolism?
Fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques.
Distal pulses in atheroembolism?
Usually remain palpable.
Hallmark digital finding of atheroembolism?
Blue toe syndrome.
Share of ischemic strokes caused by carotid disease?
Roughly 10 to 20%.
Commonest mechanism of carotid stroke?
Plaque rupture rather than occlusion with thrombosis.
Define transient ischemic attack.
Brief focal loss of neurologic function with no lasting damage; classically under 24 hours.
Define amaurosis fugax.
Transient monocular blindness, like a curtain descending.
Asymptomatic carotid disease definition window?
No stroke or transient ischemic attack in the last six months.
Most widely used initial carotid screening test?
Duplex ultrasonography.
Gold standard carotid imaging?
Digital subtraction angiography.
Screening asymptomatic adults for carotid stenosis?
Recommended against by the preventive services task force.
Stenosis threshold for surgery in symptomatic carotid disease?
Over 70%.
Asymptomatic carotid surgery criteria?
Over 80% stenosis with life expectancy over 5 years.
Gold standard procedure for high-grade carotid stenosis?
Carotid endarterectomy.
Carotid stenting suits which patients?
Poor surgical candidates.

name: Aortic Aneurysm, Pseudoaneurysm & Dissection
cards: Define an aneurysm.
Localized dilation greater than 50% of normal vessel diameter.
Diameter at which the infrarenal aorta is aneurysmal?
Over 3 cm.
Saccular versus fusiform aneurysm?
Saccular is an outpouching of part of the wall; fusiform is circumferential.
Most common site of aortic aneurysm?
The abdominal aorta.
What share of abdominal aortic aneurysms are infrarenal?
Strongest risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm?
Ever smoking.
Which population has the highest aneurysm incidence?
Caucasian men.
Three protective factors for abdominal aortic aneurysm?
Female sex, non-Caucasian race and diabetes.
Classic triad of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm?
Severe abdominal or back pain, pulsatile abdominal mass, hypotension.
Which finding is virtually diagnostic of rupture?
A pulsatile abdominal mass.
Define Grey Turner sign.
Flank ecchymosis from retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
Initial screening study for abdominal aortic aneurysm?
Abdominal ultrasound.
Best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study for an aneurysm?
Computed tomography angiography.
Surveillance for a 3.0 to 3.9 cm aneurysm?
Ultrasound every three years.
Surveillance for a 4.0 to 5.4 cm aneurysm?
Ultrasound or computed tomography every 6 to 12 months.
Elective repair threshold in women?
5.0 cm or larger.
Rapid growth that mandates abdominal aneurysm repair?
0.5 cm in six months.
Vascular specialist referral size for aortic aneurysm?
4.5 cm or larger.
Aneurysmal pain at any size calls for what?
Urgent vascular referral.
Two methods of aneurysm repair?
Endovascular aneurysm repair or open graft replacement.
Arch thoracic aneurysm symptom and nerve?
Hoarseness from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Chest X-ray sign of thoracic aneurysm?
Widened mediastinal shadow.
Which thoracic aneurysms are always repaired?
All symptomatic thoracic aortic aneurysms.
Ascending thoracic aneurysm repair diameter?
Over 5.5 cm.
Descending thoracic aneurysm repair diameter?
Over 6.0 cm.
Commonest site of pseudoaneurysm?
Femoral artery after cardiac catheterization.
Pseudoaneurysm under 2 cm management?
Watch and wait; it may thrombose and regress.
Pseudoaneurysm procedure to seal the leak?
Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection.
Pain of aortic dissection?
Sudden, severe, tearing or ripping chest pain.
Classic cause of medial degeneration in dissection?
Marfan syndrome.
Systolic target in acute aortic dissection?
100 to 120 mmHg.
Intravenous agents named for dissection, in order?
Esmolol first; nitroprusside added if pressure stays high.

name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy & Myocarditis
cards: Most common type of cardiomyopathy?
Dilated cardiomyopathy.
Define dilated cardiomyopathy.
Dilation and impaired contraction of one or both ventricles.
Shape of the heart after dilated remodeling?
Globular.
Which valve regurgitation appears first in dilated cardiomyopathy?
Mitral regurgitation.
Typical age range at presentation of dilated cardiomyopathy?
20 to 60 years.
Share of dilated cardiomyopathy that is familial?
Up to 35%.
Nutritional deficiency causing dilated cardiomyopathy?
Thiamine, vitamin B1.
Alcohol cardiomyopathy: can function recover?
Yes, if alcohol intake is reduced or stopped.
Timing of peripartum cardiomyopathy?
Last trimester to six months postpartum.
Heart sound in dilated cardiomyopathy?
S3 gallop.
Apical impulse in dilated cardiomyopathy?
Laterally displaced.
Define hepatojugular reflux.
Neck-vein distension with firm pressure over the liver.
What does a normal electrocardiogram do for dilated cardiomyopathy?
Almost rules it out.
Prominent echo feature of dilated cardiomyopathy?
Dilated, thin walls.
Define Kerley B lines.
1 to 2 cm horizontal lines meeting the pleura; pulmonary edema.
B-type natriuretic peptide level that makes heart failure unlikely?
Below 100 pg/mL.
Two drug classes every dilated cardiomyopathy patient gets?
A beta blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
Defibrillator threshold in dilated cardiomyopathy?
Ejection fraction below 35% after maximum medical therapy.
Two indications for a left ventricular assist device?
Bridge to transplant or recovery, or destination therapy.
Sodium restriction in dilated cardiomyopathy?
Less than 2 grams per day.
Five-year mortality once symptoms emerge?
Primary indication for cardiac transplantation?
Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy.
Define myocarditis.
Inflammatory disease of the myocardium.
Presumed commonest cause of myocarditis in developed countries?
Viral infection.
Who is particularly susceptible to myocarditis?
Young males.
Typical history before viral myocarditis?
A flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks earlier.
Gold standard test for myocarditis?
Endomyocardial biopsy.
Which imaging shows the extent of myocardial inflammation?
Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging.
Mainstay of myocarditis treatment?
Supportive care.
Fraction of mild myocarditis that later becomes dilated cardiomyopathy?
One third.

name: Hypertrophic, Restrictive & Stress Cardiomyopathy
cards: Define hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Left ventricular hypertrophy without a causative hemodynamic factor.
Region most often hypertrophied in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
The interventricular septum.
Inheritance of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
Autosomal dominant.
Prevalence of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
1 in 500 people.
Leading cause of sudden death in preadolescents and adolescents?
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Define systolic anterior motion.
The anterior mitral leaflet is pulled into the outflow tract.
Common presenting symptom of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
Dyspnea.
Symptom marking high sudden-death risk that needs urgent work-up?
Syncope.
Define pulsus bisferiens.
An arterial pulse with a double systolic peak.
Outflow murmur location in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
Left sternal border, 3rd or 4th intercostal space.
Does the obstructive murmur radiate to the carotids?
No; it radiates to the suprasternal notch.
Maneuvers that soften the obstructive murmur?
Squatting, passive leg raising and handgrip.
Maneuvers that increase the obstructive murmur?
Valsalva, standing and amyl nitrite.
Test of choice for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
Echocardiography.
Wall thickness confirming hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
1.5 cm or more, unexplained.
Initial drug for outflow tract obstruction?
A beta blocker.
Drug classes to avoid in outflow obstruction?
Preload or afterload reducers and positive inotropes.
Antiarrhythmic proven to reduce sudden cardiac death here?
Amiodarone.
Two septal reduction procedures?
Surgical myectomy and alcohol septal ablation.
Activity advice in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
Regular mild to moderate exercise; strenuous or competitive sport by shared decision; stay hydrated.
Least common cardiomyopathy?
Restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Most common cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy in the United States?
Amyloidosis.
Define Kussmaul sign.
Paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration.
Electrocardiogram finding of cardiac amyloidosis?
Low QRS voltage.
Test that helps separate restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis?
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging; a thickened pericardium points to constriction.
Diuretic caution in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
Lowering preload can drop output from stiff ventricles.
Prognosis of restrictive cardiomyopathy?
The poorest of all heart muscle diseases.
Who gets Takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
Postmenopausal women, 90% of cases.
Trigger of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
A significant emotional or physical stressor.
Echo finding in Takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
Mid and apical left ventricular hypokinesis or akinesis.
How is Takotsubo cardiomyopathy confirmed?
Cardiac catheterization showing normal coronary arteries.
Initial management of suspected Takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
Follow acute coronary syndrome protocols.
Cardiomyopathy strategy for adolescents?
Genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and activity restriction if high risk.
Cardiomyopathy focus in the elderly?
Tailored therapy, cautious diuretics, symptom control and palliative discussions.
